title: The Scale of Perfection
author: Walter Hilton (d. 1396)
translator: Edited and modernised from manuscript sources by Evelyn Underhill

summary: A fourteenth-century guide written for an anchoress. Book I, chapters 10 and 11, deal directly with seen light: 'if it be so, that thou see any manner of light or brightness with thy bodily eye, or in imagining, other than every man may see', or hear sounds, or feel heat in the breast like fire, the reader is to watch what it does to the heart. If it draws her from prayer and makes her want only to keep it, it is suspect and to be refused; if after initial stirring it leaves her more able to pray, it may be received with thanks but not sought. Book II describes a deliberate entry into a 'lighty murkness' by withdrawing the mind from all bodily things, and warns of a counterfeit light shown 'between two black rainy clouds'.
why_relevant: Explicit instruction on what to do when light is seen with the bodily eye or in imagination, with a test for telling good from bad; one of the clearest Western warnings and it distinguishes the two modes in so many words.
